What I learned from creating that evidence, written with Situation, Task, Action and Result.

Reflection on Coding my CV in Markdown (STAR)

Situation

During the development of my digital portfolio, I was required to create and code my CV using Markdown language. At first, I was not very familiar with Markdown and had only basic knowledge about formatting text. I realized that this task would require me to learn a new skill and apply it professionally. I also needed to ensure that my CV was well-structured, clear, and visually appealing when viewed on GitHub. This was important because my digital portfolio represents my professional identity and work readiness.

In addition, I understood that Markdown is widely used by developers and IT professionals, so learning this skill would be beneficial for my future career. I wanted to make sure that my CV looked professional and easy to read, while also demonstrating my technical abilities.

Task

My task was to learn Markdown and use it to create a professional CV. I needed to structure my document properly using headings, bullet points, bold text, links, and spacing. I also needed to make sure that my CV included important sections such as:

  • Personal Information
  • Contact Details
  • Education
  • Skills
  • Projects
  • Work Experience
  • References

I also needed to ensure that the document displayed correctly on GitHub and that it looked clean and professional.

Action

To complete this task, I started by researching Markdown syntax and learning how it works. I practiced using headings, bullet points, bold text, and spacing. I also explored how to add links and organize content properly. I reviewed examples of professional CVs written in Markdown and used them as a guide.

I also tested my Markdown file multiple times on GitHub to ensure that everything displayed correctly. I made several improvements to the layout and formatting to make the CV more readable and professional. I ensured consistency in spacing, headings, and formatting throughout the document.

During this process, I also learned:

  • How to structure professional documents
  • How to format content using Markdown
  • How to create clean and readable layouts
  • How to improve readability and presentation
  • How to use GitHub effectively

What Was Easy

Some parts of Markdown were easy to learn, such as creating headings, bullet points, and bold text. Once I understood the basic syntax, it became easier to organize my CV. Adding sections and formatting text was also simple after some practice.

What Was Difficult

Some parts were challenging, especially when formatting spacing and ensuring everything displayed correctly on GitHub. At times, I struggled with aligning content and making the document look professional. Learning how to add links and maintain consistent formatting also required extra effort. However, with practice and testing, I was able to overcome these challenges.

Result

As a result, I successfully created a professional CV using Markdown. My document became well-structured, easy to read, and visually appealing. I gained confidence in using Markdown and improved my technical skills. I also developed a better understanding of how developers present documentation professionally.

This experience helped me improve my attention to detail, formatting skills, and overall professionalism. I am now more confident in using Markdown for future projects and documentation.

Reflection on Mock Interview Video (STAR)

Situation

As part of the digital portfolio, I was required to record a mock interview video. This task allowed me to simulate a real job interview and evaluate my communication skills. At first, I felt nervous because speaking in front of the camera can be challenging. However, I understood that this was an opportunity to improve my confidence and professional communication skills.

The mock interview required me to introduce myself, discuss my skills, and explain my career goals. This experience helped me understand what employers look for during interviews.

Task

My task was to prepare for the mock interview and record a professional video. I needed to:

  • Introduce myself clearly
  • Talk about my background
  • Discuss my skills
  • Explain my career goals

I also needed to ensure that the video quality was good and that I recorded in a quiet environment.

Action

To prepare for the mock interview, I practiced answering common interview questions. I also prepared what I wanted to say about my skills, education, and career goals. I ensured that I dressed professionally and chose a quiet environment for recording.

During the video, I introduced myself and spoke about my studies in Information and Communication Technology. I discussed my skills, including technical skills and soft skills. I also spoke about my passion for technology and my career goals.

I made sure to:

After recording, I reviewed the video and made improvements where necessary.

What Was Difficult

Recording the video was challenging at first because I felt nervous speaking in front of the camera. Maintaining confidence and speaking fluently without hesitation was also difficult. However, after practicing and recording more than once, I became more comfortable and confident.

Result

The mock interview helped me improve my communication and presentation skills. I became more confident speaking professionally and presenting myself. I also identified areas where I can improve, such as reducing nervousness and speaking more confidently.

This experience prepared me for real job interviews and improved my professional readiness. I gained confidence and learned how to present myself professionally.

Agile Portfolio: Industry Placement (PRP370S)

Team CharterUser Stories & TasksProduct BacklogSprint BacklogAgile Logbook

This semester’s work: my team’s Agile process on the CivicFix project, from the team charter to the logbook.

Industry Placement. CivicFix is the current project I am working on in the company (Capaciti Data Academy, Team “The Transformers”). This section follows Collect, Select, Reflect, Connect: each artefact is followed by a reflection.

About the project

City departments receive hazard reports (potholes, broken water mains, illegal dumping, faulty traffic lights) as messy emails, blurry photos and vague locations. CivicFix turns a resident’s photo and location into a classified, located, prioritised and routed maintenance ticket, while municipal staff keep final control. The current build is a working demo that uses example presets for hazard suggestions; live image AI and municipal integration are planned.

1. Agile Team Charter

Evidence

Purpose
Turn a resident’s photo of a hazard into a verified, prioritised ticket that reaches the correct municipal department, and give staff a clear, ranked queue.
Success
A working demo, documentation and presentation by 30 October 2026, with acceptance tests (UAT-01 to UAT-13) so “working” is checked, not assumed.
Core values
Honesty, responsibility, respect, ownership, collaboration and a learning mindset.
Team memberRoleKey responsibilities
Inga PlatiGroup leaderStand-up and sprint planning, requirements, board and logbook, presentation
Anele JavuBackendAPI, database, routing logic, AI model integration, deployment
Olona WilliamsResearchLiterature review, hazard knowledge base, routing rules, photo collection and labelling, safety and privacy (POPIA) checks
Mpho ShiangFrontendReporting flow, My Reports, staff live queue, community page, map
Result MhlongoTestingAcceptance tests, model evaluation, usability testing, issue list

Ways of working

  • Framework: a short sprint (25 September to 30 October 2026) on a Trello Kanban board, using Scrum ceremonies.
  • Ceremonies: daily stand-up at 09:30, sprint planning on 25 September, review/demo before the presentation, and a retrospective at the end.
  • Communication: Teams channel for project posts and files, WhatsApp for quick updates, replies within 2 to 3 hours in core hours.
  • Decisions: consensus first; if stuck, the group leader decides after hearing everyone and records the reason.
  • Definition of Done: acceptance criteria met, works on a teammate’s machine, pushed to GitHub, no personal data or keys, documents clear and referenced, task card ticked.
  • Boundaries: not an official City or emergency service, no claiming unbuilt features, no real personal data in the repository.
  • Risks covered: absence, connectivity, backend readiness, wrong AI output, photo privacy and time pressure.
CivicFix_Agile_Team_Charter.pdf · 6 pages · signed 21 October 2026

Scroll to read all 6 pages of the signed charter. Download the PDF

Reflection (STAR method)

Situation

When our CAPACITI team of five met on 25 September to start CivicFix, I had never written a team charter before. I honestly thought it was just a form you fill in so the lecturer is happy. We were also still getting to know each other’s working styles, and even our first meeting time had to move from 10:30 to 14:30 so that everyone could attend. That small change showed me how easily a team gets out of sync when nothing is written down.

Task

My task was to help the team agree on how we would work together and to make sure my own role as the researcher was clear. That meant the literature review, the hazard knowledge base, the routing rules, collecting and labelling Cape Town photos and checking the POPIA and privacy rules. I also had to read the finished charter properly before signing it, because my signature means I agree to follow it.

Action

We built the charter section by section. I gave input on the purpose and the success definition, and I helped most with the boundaries and risks, because those touch on research and privacy: no real personal data in the repository, not presenting CivicFix as an official City service, and not claiming features we have not built. We agreed on a stand-up at 09:30, Teams and WhatsApp for communication, and a Definition of Done that includes working on a teammate’s machine and being pushed to GitHub.

The first version was agreed on 25 September, it was written up in full as version 1.1 on 9 October, and all five of us signed it on 21 October. I also used it in my logbooks. When I wrote about connectivity problems or the backend not being ready, I was pointing to risks we had already listed in the charter.

What Was Easy

Describing my role was easy because I already knew what research the team needed. The values were easy too. Honesty, respect and ownership were things everyone cared about.

What Was Difficult

It was harder to turn good intentions into rules we can really follow. Deciding what “done” means and what counts as a blocker took a few rounds of discussion. Finding times that suit five people, and keeping the review of the charter short, was also a challenge.

Result

The charter gave us something to point to when things got busy. When we were unsure how to describe the demo, our own boundaries answered the question, so we say clearly that live AI and municipal systems are not connected. I learned that a charter is a living agreement that should be reviewed at every retrospective, and I feel more confident about helping to set up a team properly in my industry placement.

Reflection (STAR method)

Situation

After the charter, we had to describe what CivicFix must do from the point of view of the people who will use it. I knew what a feature was, but I was used to thinking “we need a map and an upload page” and not “who needs this and why”. The user story format, As a… I want… so that…, was new to me in a real project.

Task

My task was to help write the user stories on our Trello cards and to break each one into smaller checklist steps with a named owner. Later, in the requirements stage, I also had to help create stories for residents and municipal staff and link them to my hazard knowledge base and routing rules.

Action

Our first cards were written as team stories. Card 1, for example, says that as a project group we wanted to identify a problem affecting our community so that we could develop a useful web-based solution. Each story had a checklist of about four or five steps and every step was given to one person. My steps included researching how these issues affect residents on card 1 and identifying who is affected on card 2.

For the user stories card on 12 October, I linked each story to a hazard type and to the department that should receive it. I also checked that the privacy story about blurring faces and number plates had real criteria, such as removing metadata that is not needed. After that the team wrote the product stories US-01 to US-09, each with acceptance criteria.

What Was Easy

Writing the “As a… I want…” sentence came easily once I knew the users: residents who report hazards, dispatchers, reviewers and community members. Ticking off the checklist items on Trello was also satisfying, because it showed our progress straight away.

What Was Difficult

Acceptance criteria were the hardest part. Something like “the system works well” cannot be tested, so I had to learn to write measurable ones, such as 250 metres for the duplicate check and a confidence level of about 70% for human review. It was also hard to make sure everyone read the stories in the same way, and I wrote that down as a blocker in my logbook on 12 October.

Result

The stories gave the team a shared picture of who we are building for, and they became the base for our acceptance tests. I learned that a story starts a conversation and is not a full specification, and that good criteria save a lot of time later. I can now break a requirement into small tasks, which is a skill I want to use in my industry placement.

Reflection (STAR method)

Situation

By the second week we had a long list of things CivicFix could do: the reporting flow, the duplicate check, My Reports, a staff queue, a community page, AI classification, and even ideas like WhatsApp reporting and other languages. I realised quickly that we could not build all of it in a short sprint, so we needed one ordered list showing what comes first.

Task

My task was to help build and order the product backlog on Trello and to give input on the research items, such as the literature review, the hazard knowledge base, the routing rules and the photo collection. I also took part in defining the project scope and in prioritising the features with the MoSCoW method.

Action

Our board has a Product Backlog list that cards are pulled from into the sprint. It starts with problem identification and research, then moves through requirements, design, development and testing, up to the documentation, the presentation and the logbook.

On 10 October we defined the scope. The resident reporting flow, My Reports, the staff live queue, crew assignment and the community page are in, and live image AI and municipal systems are not connected. On 11 October I took part in the MoSCoW prioritisation and gave my view on which hazard types and routing rules are must-haves, so that the first version recognises the hazards residents report most, such as potholes and broken water mains.

What Was Easy

Listing the work was easy because it followed the steps we had already completed. Watching items move from the backlog to the sprint and then to completed was also motivating.

What Was Difficult

The hard part was agreeing on what is a Must have and what is only a Should have, because everybody had a feature they cared about. Estimating how long things would take was difficult as well, since many of us are still learning parts of the stack.

Result

The backlog kept us focused and honest about what is and is not included. I learned that prioritising means saying “not yet” to good ideas, and that the order should change when we learn something new. Next time I would review it more often, for example after the testing stage.

Reflection (STAR method)

Situation

Once the requirements were finished, the team had to turn the backlog into a plan for the weeks ahead. The sprint is short and the programme also has a daily Coursera AI course, so time was always tight and the sprint goal had to be realistic.

Task

My task was to take part in sprint planning, pick up the cards that belong to the research role and keep my progress updated on the sprint list.

Action

We pulled cards into the Sprint list one at a time, each with a label, dates and a checklist where every step has an owner. In the first part of the sprint we completed the discovery cards, from defining the project objectives on 25 September to the problem statement on 30 September and the project goals on 1 October. After the requirements cards (13 to 16), we moved on to the design review on 21 October, set up the development environment on 22 October, organised the project files on 23 October and prepared the development plan on 24 October.

I saved my research documents, the hazard knowledge base, the routing rules and the labelled photos in shared folders with clear names, and I made sure no real personal data was saved there. At the moment the team is working on the card to enhance the CivicFix prototype (27 to 28 October), and the cards to fix issues, deploy and present are planned for November.

What Was Easy

Moving cards across the board and ticking checklist items was easy, and it gave a clear picture of who was doing what.

What Was Difficult

Planning around the backend was difficult. The frontend needs the backend, and when the backend is not ready, work slows down for everybody. We also lost time to connectivity problems at CAPACITI and to coordinating group schedules, especially on the weekends when we work remotely.

Result

The sprint backlog made it clear what the team had finished and what was still open. I learned that a sprint plan is only as good as its dependencies, so asking for a backend status at every stand-up, as our charter says, is not just a formality. I also learned that it is better to say a card is still in progress than to tick it too early.

Reflection (STAR method)

Situation

From 25 September the team held a stand-up every day at 09:30, and each of us had to keep a personal logbook for it. At first it looked like extra paperwork. Then I realised that a record of my progress and my problems is also my evidence of how I contributed to a group project.

Task

My task was to complete four logbooks, one for each stand-up period (25 to 30 September, 9 to 12 October, 21 to 24 October and 13 to 16 November), using the CAPACITI template. Each logbook has a taskboard, a walkthrough of the team’s flow and daily answers to three questions: what I completed, what I plan to do next and what is blocking me.

Action

Every day I linked my answers to a Trello card. In logbook 1, for example, I recorded the first meeting and sprint planning, my research on how hazard reports reach municipal departments, the target users we identified (residents and municipal staff) and my contribution to the problem statement. In logbook 2 I wrote about my input on the non-functional requirements, the scope, the MoSCoW priorities and the user stories. In logbook 3 I recorded the design review, setting up my development environment and organising the project files.

In every entry I wrote my blockers honestly, such as finding reliable sources specific to Cape Town, coordinating group schedules and balancing the project with the daily Coursera course. Logbook 4 covers the last period, and I will complete it when those days have passed.

What Was Easy

Writing what I had completed was easy because every task matched a card and its checklist. After a few days the three questions became a habit.

What Was Difficult

It was hard to find the energy to write the logbook at the end of a busy day, and it takes some honesty to write down a problem instead of saying everything is fine. I also had to check that my dates matched the Trello board.

Result

My logbooks give a day-by-day picture of how the team moved from the problem to the users, the requirements and the design, and they show my own part as the researcher. I learned that blockers shared early are easier to fix, and that a short daily record helps me reflect and plan. I will keep using this habit in my industry placement.

Connecting it all

The five artefacts form one chain: the charter sets how the team works, the user stories (and the Trello cards behind them) say what users need, the product backlog orders that work, the sprint backlog commits to a slice of it, and the logbook records what really happened and what we learned. Together they show my growth from following a process to understanding why each part exists.

References: CivicFix Project Documentation (15 October 2026); CivicFix presentation, The Transformers (16 October 2026); CivicFix Agile Team Charter v1.1 (signed 21 October 2026).

Overall Reflection

This project helped me grow both technically and professionally. I learned new skills such as Markdown coding, GitHub usage, and creating a digital portfolio. I also improved my communication skills through the mock interview video.

The experience prepared me for the workplace and helped me understand how to present myself professionally. I am now more confident in my abilities and ready to apply these skills in my future career.

This semester I added Agile practice to that foundation. Working on CivicFix with a team charter, user stories, backlogs and a logbook showed me how to plan, communicate and reflect as part of a team, which is exactly what I will do in my industry placement.

This digital portfolio represents my growth, learning, and readiness for the professional world.
